questions.stem: Which query correctly finds a category in the 'Commodity' table that has more than 5 products with a Price greater than 600?
options: SELECT category FROM Commodity GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*)>5 AND Price >600;
SELECT category FROM Commodity WHERE Price>600 GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*)>5;
SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM Commodity GROUP BY Category HAVING Price>600 AND COUNT(*)>5;
SELECT category FROM Commodity GROUP BY HAVING COUNT(Price>600)>5;
questions.reason: Served rows work exactly this shape (row filter in WHERE, COUNT condition in HAVING after GROUP BY) and state the WHERE/HAVING rule.

match.stem:
The table EMP is given below.
Empid | Ename | Dept | Salary
101 | Ravi | Sales | 45000
102 | Meena | HR | 52000
103 | Arjun | Sales | NULL
104 | Kavya | IT | 61000
105 | Imran | HR | 48000
What is the output of the query: SELECT Dept, SUM(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE Salary > 45000 GROUP BY Dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
match.explanation: WHERE Salary > 45000 removes Ravi (45000) and the NULL row, leaving Meena (52000), Kavya (61000) and Imran (48000). GROUP BY forms HR with 52000 + 48000 = 100000 and IT with 61000. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only HR, so the output is HR 100000.

match.stem:
Arrange the following searches in increasing order of the number of comparisons they need in the worst case. Binary search is applied to a sorted list.
(A) Linear search on a list of 64 elements
(B) Binary search on a sorted list of 64 elements
(C) Linear search on a list of 8 elements
(D) Binary search on a sorted list of 8 elements
match.explanation: Binary search needs at most floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons in the worst case, which is 4 for 8 elements and 7 for 64. Linear search needs n comparisons in the worst case, which is 8 for the list of 8 and 64 for the list of 64. The increasing order is therefore (D), (B), (C), (A).

Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, insertion sort places each element into the sorted part, and binary search is a searching method.
